title: Alert Triage and Ticketing
unit: CS-ICT251101 Monitor and Report Cyber Threats

parts.html:
At the end of this session, you should be able to:

  1. Explain the three pre-identified criteria in the Competency Standards: threat, detection and routine.
  2. Assess an alert step by step: routine check, detection, threat level, asset tier and priority (PC 1.4).
  3. Tell a true positive from a false positive or routine activity using evidence, not the rule name.
  4. Issue a complete incident ticket upon confirmation of detection, linking related alerts and reports (PC 1.5).
  5. Prioritize the work queue with a priority matrix and response targets.

Yesterday you received alerts and reports and checked them for red flags (PC 1.1–1.3). Today you assess each one against pre-identified criteria (PC 1.4) and issue a ticket when the detection is confirmed (PC 1.5). This is called triage, the same word hospitals use when a nurse decides which patient the doctor sees first. In the lab you follow SOC-SOP-02 Alert Assessment and Ticketing (~/day6/soc_triage_sop.txt), always in this order:

  1. Routine — is it expected, approved activity? If yes, record it with its RT code and stop.
  2. Detection — what does the evidence show happened: confirmed, blocked, or a false positive?
  3. Threat — how dangerous is it: critical, high, medium or low?
  4. Asset — how important is the affected computer: Tier 1, 2 or 3?
  5. Priority and ticket — read the priority from the matrix, and issue a ticket if the detection is confirmed.

The Competency Standards list three kinds of pre-identified criteria: routine, detection and threat. "Pre-identified" means they are written in the SOP before any alert arrives, so every analyst judges alerts the same way.

Routine Criteria (check first)

CodeRoutine Activity (SOC-SOP-02 STEP 1)
RT1Security solution updates (Defender signatures, Wazuh rules)
RT2Internal vulnerability scans from SCAN-01 (10.10.1.60), Tuesday and Thursday 08:00–10:00
RT3External scan by the approved vendor from 198.51.100.23, Thursday 09:00–11:00 (CHG-1142)
RT4Backups by scbackup.exe (SafeCopy, signed)
RT5Work covered by an APPROVED change: same host, same person, inside the change window
RT6Agent keep-alive and health messages

Detection Criteria

DetectionMeaningExample from the Lab
Confirmed (true positive)The malicious activity happened: the program ran, the logon succeeded, data left, files changedQ-5001: 18 failed logons, then a successful one
BlockedA real attempt that a security solution stopped before it took effectQ-5004: SQL injection answered with 403
False positiveThe alert fired, but the activity was not maliciousB-03: "impossible travel" through the company VPN
NOTE — Read the details, not only the rule name
The rule name says what the tool suspected; the details say what happened. "Virus detected" can be IT's approved antivirus test (routine), and "Trojan quarantined" can be dangerous if the user restored it and ran it. Red flags (ransomware, PE infection) always count as Confirmed, even when one step was blocked.

Threat Criteria

Threat LevelMeaningExample
CriticalA red flag: ransomware or PE infection (SOC-SOP-01 Section C)Mass rename to .lockd
HighConfirmed compromise of an account or host, or sensitive data that leftPayroll file uploaded to a personal drive
MediumAn attack attempt that was blocked or failed; malware quarantined before it ranTrojan quarantined on download
LowNuisance: unwanted apps (PUA), adware, internet noise blocked at the edgePUA installer blocked

parts.h: 3. Asset Tiers and the Priority Matrix
parts.html:
The same threat matters more on a more important computer. The asset inventory (~/day6/asset_inventory.csv) gives every computer a tier. Always use the AFFECTED computer, not the device that raised the alert: a firewall alert about a marketing PC is about the marketing PC.

TierExamples
Tier 1Business-critical: domain controller, core banking, payroll, servers, public website, internet firewall
Tier 2Business computers: staff workstations and laptops
Tier 3Low impact: isolated test and lab machines
ThreatTier 1Tier 2Tier 3
CriticalP1P1P1
HighP1P2P2
MediumP2P3P3
LowP3P4P4
  • P1 — respond within 15 minutes and call the Shift Lead
  • P2 — within 1 hour
  • P3 — within 4 hours
  • P4 — next business day
  • Priority is set for Confirmed and Blocked alerts; false positives and routine alerts get none.

A ticket is the official record of an incident in the ticketing system. The Competency Standards say a ticket is issued upon confirmation of detection, so blocked attempts, false positives and routine alerts are recorded in the shift log instead.

RuleWhat to Do
T1Confirmed → issue an incident ticket
T2One ticket per incident: link every alert and report about the same incident to it
T3Blocked → shift log with its priority (ticket only if the Shift Lead asks)
T4False positive → shift log, and request rule tuning
T5Routine → shift log with the RT code
Ticket FieldWhat to Write
Ticket ID and titleINC-20261105-101 · "Ransomware activity on FIN-PC-03"
Linked alerts and reportsEvery alert ID and report ID about this incident
Affected assetHost, role and tier
Category and priorityRansomware / PE infection / Account compromise / Data leak / Malware · P1–P4
EvidenceThe facts that confirm the detection: counts, names, times
Actions takenWhat Level I already did, e.g. "user told to unplug the network cable"
Assigned to and statusShift Lead (P1), Tier 2 analyst (P2–P3), IT Helpdesk (P4) · New
TIP — One incident, one ticket
On FIN-PC-03 the EDR saw a mass rename (Q-5005), then a shadow copy deletion (Q-5011), and the user phoned the SOC (IR-01). That is one incident, so it gets one ticket with all three linked. Write facts, not guesses, and never put passwords or unnecessary personal data in a ticket (Data Privacy Act, RA 10173).

• Trusting the rule name or the vendor severity without reading the details
  • Forgetting the routine list and the change calendar (only APPROVED changes count)
  • Using the tier of the device that raised the alert instead of the affected computer
  • Opening a ticket for a blocked attempt, or several tickets for one incident
  • Closing an incident ticket: Level I opens and hands over; it never closes

TermMeaning
TriageSorting alerts so that the most urgent real threats are handled first
Pre-identified criteriaRules written in the SOP in advance: routine, detection and threat
True positiveAn alert about something malicious that really happened (Confirmed)
False positiveAn alert that fired on harmless activity
Asset tierHow important a computer is to the business (Tier 1 most important)
PriorityHow fast to respond (P1–P4), from threat × asset tier
Change calendarThe list of approved planned work; it explains many "suspicious" alerts
TicketThe official record of one incident, with all linked alerts and reports

• TESDA Competency Standards — Cyber Threat Monitoring Level I (ICT Sector), unit CS-ICT251101, Element 1 and Range of Variables 4.

  • ITIL® 4 Incident Management practice (priority from impact and urgency).
  • MITRE ATT&CK® Framework — attack.mitre.org.
  • Republic Act No. 10173 (Data Privacy Act of 2012) and Republic Act No. 10175 (Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012).
